corrected_value.title: Wnt activity defines colon cancer stem cells and is regulated by the microenvironment
corrected_value.authors: Vermeulen; De Sousa E Melo; van der Heijden; Cameron; de Jong; Borovski; Tuynman; Todaro; Merz; Rodermond; Sprick; Kemper; Richel; Stassi; Medema

decisions.quote:
As part of the
Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology
we published a Registered Report (Evans et al., 2015), that described how we intended to replicate selected experiments from the paper ‘Wnt activity defines colon cancer stem cells and is regulated by the microenvironment’ (Vermeulen et al., 2010). Here, we report the results.
decisions.reason: The paper explicitly identifies Vermeulen et al. (2010), 'Wnt activity defines colon cancer stem cells and is regulated by the microenvironment' (Nature Cell Biology 12:468-476, doi:10.1038/ncb2048), as the original study whose experiments (Figures 2F, 6D, and 7E) are replicated. Evans et al. (2015) is the Stage 1 Registered Report protocol for this replication rather than an independent original target. Both shipped and blind codings accurately identify this original study.

decisions.quote:
Using three independent primary spheroidal colon cancer cultures that expressed a Wnt reporter construct we observed high Wnt activity was associated with the cell surface markers CD133, CD166, and CD29, but not CD24 and CD44, while the original study found all five markers were correlated with high Wnt activity (Figure 2F; Vermeulen et al., 2010). Clonogenicity was highest in cells with high Wnt activity and clonogenic potential of cells with low Wnt activity were increased by myofibroblast-secreted factors, including HGF. While the effects were in the same direction as the original study (Figure 6D; Vermeulen et al., 2010) whether statistical significance was reached among the different conditions varied. When tested
in vivo
, we did not find a difference in tumorigenicity between high and low Wnt activity, while the original study found cells with high Wnt activity were more effective in inducing tumors (Figure 7E; Vermeulen et al., 2010).
decisions.reason: Across the three replicated figure panels of Vermeulen et al. (2010), the authors report mixed results without a single overarching success or failure verdict: high Wnt activity was associated with CD133, CD166, and CD29, and in vitro clonogenicity effects were in the same direction as the original study (with varying statistical significance across cultures), whereas CD24 and CD44 were not associated with high Wnt activity and in vivo tumorigenicity did not differ between high and low Wnt activity in contrast to the original study.

decisions.reason: The study collected new experimental data using three independent primary spheroidal colon cancer cultures in flow cytometry, limiting-dilution clonogenicity, and mouse xenograft tumorigenicity assays to re-test the published findings of Vermeulen et al. (2010), making it a replication.
